title: How to Pray With Your Kids at Bedtime
excerpt: Bedtime is the one moment a child is finally still. Use it to teach them that the last voice before sleep speaks to a Father who never sleeps.
body:
There is a window at the end of the day when a child stops moving. The toys are down, the lights are low, the resistance has drained out of them. For most of childhood this is the one reliable moment of stillness you will get, and it is handed to you every single night. The question is what fills it. A screen. A rushed exit. Or a prayer.

Bedtime prayer is the easiest family discipleship to begin and the easiest to skip, because no one is watching and the child will not protest if you drop it. That is exactly why it matters. What we do when only God sees is what actually forms us.

## Why the last words of the day carry weight

The Psalms are full of the night. "I will both lie down and sleep, for you alone, O Lord, make me dwell in safety." "On my bed I remember you; I think of you through the watches of the night." The ancient instinct was to give the dark to God before sleep took you, because the dark is where a child's fears live. The monster, the bad dream, the worry they cannot name. Bedtime prayer does not pretend those fears away. It hands them to someone stronger.

Your child learns their theology of God less from what you teach in daylight than from what you do with their fear at night. Teach them that the last voice they hear speaks to a Father who is awake while they sleep.

## A simple pattern that lasts for years

Keep it the same most nights, because the repetition is the teaching. A pattern a child can predict becomes a pattern a child can pray alone when you are not there.

Start by thanking God for one good thing from the day. Ask the child to name it. You will be surprised what they choose, and you will learn what their day actually held.

Then say sorry for one thing. Not an interrogation. Just, "Was there anything today you wish you had done differently?" This teaches confession as a normal part of being loved, not a punishment. Most adults never learned this, and it shows.

Then ask God for help with one thing tomorrow. The spelling test. Being kind to the brother they fought with. Courage for the thing they dread.

Then bless them. Lay a hand on their head and say words over them. "The Lord bless you and keep you." The old Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6 has been spoken over children for three thousand years. Speak it over yours.

## Pray honest, not pretty

The temptation is to perform a prayer, to make it sound finished and warm. Children see through it instantly. Pray the way you would speak to your own father. Short sentences. Real concerns. If the day was hard, say so to God in front of them. If you were short-tempered, let them hear you ask forgiveness. A child who hears a parent confess to God learns that grace is for the people who need it, which is everyone.

I have prayed beautiful nonsense over a sleeping child and meant none of it. I have also prayed three broken sentences over a frightened one and watched the fear let go. The second kind is the kind that forms a soul.

## Teach them to pray, then let them

The goal is not to be the family chaplain forever. The goal is a child who one day prays without you. So hand it over slowly. Let them thank God in their own words. Let them name their own worry. The prayers will be strange and long and full of dogs and dinosaurs, and you will let them run, because a child learning to talk to God is more important than a tidy bedtime.

Do not correct the theology of a four-year-old's prayer. Correct nothing. Let them speak. The accuracy comes later. The habit comes first.

## This week

Tonight, sit on the edge of the bed instead of calling goodnight from the door. Thank God for one thing your child names. Say sorry for one thing. Ask help for tomorrow. Then put your hand on their head and bless them by name with the words of Numbers 6. Do it again tomorrow, and the night after. Within a week your child will start to expect it, and the expectation is the gift. You are teaching them that the day does not close until it has been handed to God.

Some night years from now they will lie awake in a room you cannot reach, and the words will come back to them. That is what you are building.
